Posted July 21, 2003
Analysis by Richard Cowan

On March 26th, I wrote about how wars have unintended consequences, and in the case of Iraq, some began even before the fighting.
See
Unintended Consequences: How The Iraq War Has Changed the Global Climate for Cannabis Prohibition. Analysis by Richard Cowan

It is now clear that one of these unintended consequences has been the destruction of the credibility of both Bush and Blair, because of statements they made to justify the rush to war. Last February 14th, I raised a question about the credibility of the Bush regime, because they had lied to us about cannabis.
See
They've Lied to Us About Marijuana, So How Do We Know That They Aren't Lying About Iraq? Credibility in Time of War.

Now, it is time to turn that question around. If they have lied to us about Iraq, why should we believe what they say about cannabis? On March 11th, I raised questions about what it takes to justify a war.
See
Is the War On Drugs A Just War. "? Should It Be Easier To Justify Violence Against A Foreign Dictatorship Than Against Peaceful Citizens Of One's Own Country?

Of course, there would be absolutely no point in asking Bush and Blair these questions. Rather, we should ask the critics of Bush and Blair why knowing the truth about Saddam is more important than the truth about cannabis users, especially the medical users whom they are attacking so viciously?
See
Scottish MS Patient Says She Will Kill Herself When Trial Is Over. But GW Pharmaceutical's Research Proves That Her Death Will Really Be Murder. The Need for A Patients Rights Organization.

Last week, I noted that the new executive editor of The New York Times clearly knows that John Walters is a liar.
See
Is The New Executive Editor of The New York Times An Anti-Prohibitionist? At Least He Knows The Meaning of Reefer Madness.

But if it is wrong to lie about uranium from Niger, why isn't it wrong to lie about cannabis from Canada?
See
Dan Gardner of The Ottawa Citizen Continues Iconoclastic Practice of Questioning Government Statements And Checking Facts. Someday These Techniques May Even Be Taught In Journalism Schools.

These are questions that we should be asking not only The Times but also every columnist and reporter who raises questions about lies being told to justify one war, but not another that is even closer to home.

It is also important to note that the Bush/Blair fallback position to justify the Iraq war is that the Iraqi people have been liberated, and freedom is worth fighting for. That argument is not so easily dismissed, and perhaps it is valid. It remains to be seen if Iraq is really going to be free, and it is not clear that it was the duty of the American and British people to die to bring them freedom, but I am more than happy to agree that freedom is worth fighting for, especially at home.

And if it is wrong for illegal combatants to be denied due process, why is it acceptable for medical cannabis defendants in federal courts to be denied the right to inform juries about their medical conditions? More and more people, including the editors of The New York Times, are asking these questions.
See
Astonishing Editorial In New York Times Attacks Rosenthal Prosecution. Finally Taking The Issue Seriously?

When George Orwell was a young British imperialist official in a particularly backward part of Burma in the 1920s, he found himself compelled to kill a rampaging elephant. Later, in 1936 he described it in an essay, Killing an Elephant. He wrote, I perceived in this moment that when the white man turns tyrant it is his own freedom that he destroys. He becomes a sort of hollow, posing dummy For it is a condition of his rule that he shall spend his life in trying to impress the natives and so in every crisis he has to do what the natives expect of him. He wears a mask and his face grows into it.
(The essay can be found in Orwell and Politics, published by Penguin.)

At the strategic level, it is worth noting that Orwell also said that he had to kill the elephant after he had sent for an elephant gun. The people expected it of me and I had to do it. Similarly, Bush and Blair locked themselves into killing their elephant when they sent the troops into the Gulf. Orwell ended his essay with an insight that is far beyond Bush's capacity: I often wondered whether any of the others grasped that I had done it solely to avoid looking like a fool.
See
The 50th Anniversary of The Publishing Of Orwell's 1984
Analysis By Richard Cowan

I like to say that the reason that we anti-prohibitionist will ultimately prevail in the western democracies is that the Drug War is absolutely incompatible with the fundamental principles on which free societies are based. As Martin Luther King, Jr. observed about the civil rights movement: We will win because are not trying to get America to change it fundamental principles, but to live up to them.

We cannot go around the world and expect to be taken seriously as bringers of peace and freedom when our government brings neither at home. We cannot expect to impose democracy in Iraq, when our government tramples on democracy at home. Our government cannot expect to be believed by Iraqis, when it is not believed by its own citizens.
See
Science, Democracy, Ideology and the Prohibitionist Police State. Marijuana Use Doesn't Hurt Thinking Skills But Prohibition Does. Analysis by Richard Cowan

As the great British historian and champion of liberty, Thomas Babington Macaulay,wrote, I know of only two ways in which societies can be governed, by public opinion or by the sword.

Unfortunately, we have seen again and again that those who seek to move public opinion by lying always prefer to govern by the sword. The most important question of the day is not whether freedom will come to Baghdad, but whether it will return to Washington and London.
